<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
If $\big({\mathcal X},\tau\big)$ is a topological space and $d$ is a metric on ${\mathcal X}$ such that the metric topology $\tau_d$ generated by $d$ is contained in $\tau$, then we shall say that the metric $d$ is compatible with $\tau$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A topological space  $\big({\mathcal X},\tau\big)$ is called {\em submetric}, if there exists a metric $d$ compatible with $\tau$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{Ex:Hilb}
	Let ${\mathds{H}}$ be a separable infinite dimensional (real) Hilbert space with the inner product $\langle \cdot,\cdot\rangle$. By the weak topology $\tau_w$ on ${\mathds{H}}$ we mean the topology generated by all linear functionals $\{ \langle\cdot, y\rangle\,;\, y \in {\mathds{H}}\}$ (i.e. the coarsest topology $\tau$ such that all these functionals are $\tau$-continuous). The basis of neighborhoods of $0$ in $\tau_w$ is uncountable and so the weak topology is not metrizable (see e.g. \cite[Theorem 1, p.40]{Jar81}). On the other hand, let us take an orthonormal basis $\{e_i\}_{i\in{\mathds{N}}}$ in ${\mathds{H}}$  and define
	\[ {\mathds{H}} \times {\mathds{H}} \ni (x,y) \mapsto d(x,y) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^i} \frac{|\langle x-y, e_i\rangle|}{1 + |\langle x-y, e_i\rangle|}.\]
	It is a continuous metric on ${\mathds{H}}$. Hence $({\mathds{H}},\tau_w)$ is a submetric space. Being a linear topological space it is also a completely regular space  \cite[p.16]{Sch71}. Recall that a topological space $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is {\em completely regular} if for each $\tau$-closed set $F$ and each point $x_0\not\in F$ there exists a continuous function $f : {\mathcal X} \to [0,1]$ such that $f(x_0) = 1$ and $f(x) = 0$ if $x \in F$. We conclude that the inclusion no. 1 in the above diagram is strict.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{Ex:Smir}
	This example was constructed by Smirnov in \cite[Example 1, p. 107]{Smir51}. We shall follow the formalism of \cite{Eng89}. Let ${\mathcal X} = {\mathds{R}}^1$ and let $Z$ be the set of reciprocals of all positive integers. Consider the system of neighborhoods of $x\in {\mathds{R}}^1$ defined by
	\begin{equation}
		B(x) = \begin{cases} \{ (x-1/i,x+1/i)\,;\, i\in {\mathds{N}}\},& \text{ if $x \neq 0$}, \\
			\{ (x-1/i,x+1/i)\setminus Z\,;\, i\in {\mathds{N}}\},& \text{ if $x = 0$.}
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
	Then it was proved in \cite[Example 1.5.6, p. 39]{Eng89} that $\{B(x)\}_{x\in{\mathds{R}}^1}$ is a basis for some topology $\tau$ (the ``Smirnov topology'') and the space $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is not a regular space (hence also not a completely regular topological space).
	
	On the other hand, any interval $(-\varepsilon,+\delta)$ contains some  set $(x-1/i,x+1/i)\setminus Z$ (but not conversely), hence $\tau$ is {\em strictly} stronger than the usual - metric - topology of ${\mathds{R}}^1$. It follows that the Smirnov space is a submetric space. This proves that the inclusion no.2 in the diagram is strict.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{Ex:Tych}
	For our purposes it is enough to consider the Tychonoff cube of the weight of continuum, e.g. the Cartesian product $[0,1]^{[0,1]}$. It is a completely regular topological space by \cite[Theorem 2.3.11]{Eng89} and is not metrizable, as the basis at every $x \in [0,1]^{[0,1]}$ is uncountable. But this is not enough for our purposes. We want to show that the Tychonoff cube is not {\em submetrizable}. Assume there exists a continuous (with respect to the product topology $\tau_{\Pi}$) metric $d$ on $[0,1]^{[0,1]}$. Then the identity map $I : \big([0,1]^{[0,1]},\tau_{\Pi}\big) \to \big([0,1]^{[0,1]},\tau_d\big)$ is a continuous and one-to-one map of the compact space $\big([0,1]^{[0,1]},\tau_{\Pi}\big)$ onto the Hausdorff space $\big([0,1]^{[0,1]},\tau_d\big)$. By \cite[Theorem 3.1.13]{Eng89} the map $I$ is a homeomorphism, hence $\big([0,1]^{[0,1]},\tau_{\Pi}\big)$ is metrizable. A contradiction.  This proves that the inclusion no. 3 is strict.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Compact subsets of a submetric space are $G_{\delta}$ sets.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm_compmetr}
	Compact subsets of a submetric space are metrizable.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Note that the metric topology on a $\tau$-compact set $K$ is {\em independent} of the chosen particular metric $d$ (only compatibility with $\tau$ is required). This is the reason that, while talking on a submetric space $({\mathcal X}, \tau)$, we do not relate any explicit metric with it.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The metrizability of compact subsets is crucial for the submetric space version of the almost sure Skorokhod  representation theorem for weakly convergent sequences \cite{Jak97a}. 
	Due to its ease of applicability, this version has become a commonly used tool in studying existence problems for certain classes of stochastic partial differential equations.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Simp}
	Let $F \subset {\mathcal X}$ be $\tau$-closed. If $\{x_n\} \subset F$ and $x_n \ \mathop{\longrightarrow}_{\tau}\  x_0$, then $x_0 \in F$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm_seqcomp}
	A subset of a submetric space is compact if, and only if, it is {\em sequentially compact}.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{Rem:compare}
	Suppose we have two comparable topologies $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ on ${\mathcal X}$: $\tau_1 \subset \tau_2$. If $({\mathcal X},\tau_1)$ is submetric, then so is $({\mathcal X},\tau_2)$. 
	
	Further, suppose that any $\tau_1$-compact subset is also $\tau_2$-compact. This implies that the families ${\mathcal K}_{\tau_i} = \{ K\,|\, \text{ $K$ is  $\tau_i$-compact}\}$, $i=1,2$, coincide. 
	
	These simple facts can have important consequences in limit theorems for stochastic processes. In order  to check \emph{the uniform tightness condition} of some family $\{X_{i}\}_{i\in{\mathds{I}}}$ of random elements with values in the submetric space $({\mathcal X},\tau_1)$, one verifies whether for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a $\tau_1$-compact set  $K_{\varepsilon}$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:ut}
		{\mathbb{P}}\big( X_i \in K_{\varepsilon} \big) > 1 - \varepsilon,\qquad i\in{\mathds{I}}.
	\end{equation}
	When ${\mathcal K}_{\tau_1} = {\mathcal K}_{\tau_2}$, equation (\ref{eq:ut}) yields the uniform tightness of $\{X_{i}\}_{i\in{\mathds{I}}}$ in $({\mathcal X},\tau_2)$! Moreover, since $\tau_2 \supset \tau_1$, the larger topology $\tau_2$ provides a wider class of continuous functions, which can make the resulting limit theorem substantially richer.
	
	It is interesting that one can identify the maximal topology $\tau_2$ that satisfies the property ${\mathcal K}_{\tau_1} = {\mathcal K}_{\tau_2}$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{tauesclosed}
	Let $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ be a Hausdorff topological space. Say that $F\subset {\mathcal X}$ is $\tau_s$-closed if limits of $\tau$-convergent sequences of elements of $F$ remain in $F$, i.e. 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:closed}
		\text{if $x_n \in F, \ n=1,2,\ldots$, and $x_n\ \mathop{\longrightarrow}_{\tau}\  x_0$, then $x_0\in F$}. 
	\end{equation}
	The topology given by $\tau_s$-closed sets is called the sequential topology generated by $\tau$ and will be denoted by $\tau_s$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm_seqtopol}
	Let  $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ be a Hausdorff topological space. Then
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\tau \subset \tau_s$ (i.e. $\tau_s$ is finer than $\tau$).
		\item $x_n \ \mathop{\longrightarrow}_{\tau_s}\  x_0$ if, and only if, $x_n \ \mathop{\longrightarrow}_{\tau}\  x_0$.
	\end{enumerate}
	In particular, $\tau_s$ is Hausdorff.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{compequiv} Let $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ be a Hausdorff topological space. A subset $K \subset {\mathcal X}$ is $\tau$-sequentially compact if, and only if, it is $\tau_s$-sequentially compact.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm_finest}
	Let $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ be a submetric space. The topology $\tau_s$ is the finest topology among topologies which are finer than $\tau$ and have the same compact subsets as $\tau$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The topology $\tau_s$ can be substantially finer than the initial submetric topology $\tau$. For instance, if we start with the weak topology $\tau_w$ on a separable Hilbert space (Example \ref{Ex:Hilb}), then the sequential topology $(\tau_w)_s$ is the so-called bounded topology on ${\mathds{H}}$ (see, e.g., \cite[Section 5.5]{DunSch58}).
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{Rem:Intuition}
	Theorem \ref{thm_seqcomp} and relation (\ref{eq:2}) provide a modeling framework, which is unavailable not only within the metric regime, but also in the broader context of completely regular spaces with metrizable compacts \cite{SmFo76}. Specifically, we refer to sequential spaces generated by ${\mathcal L}$-convergences.  We will focus only on intuition and will not develop the formal theory here, referring instead to \cite[Section 6]{Jak18} for all necessary concepts and results.
	
	Imagine a space ${\mathcal X}$ within which we are given a family ${\mathcal C}$ of checkable conditions ``suspected" for forming criteria of compactness in some topology. Suppose we are able to find a convergence of sequences $\mathop{\longrightarrow}$ of elements of ${\mathcal X}$ such that any set $C$ satisfying the conditions ${\mathcal C}$ is relatively compact with respect to $\mathop{\longrightarrow}$. If there exists a countable family $\{f_i\}$ of {\em sequentially} continuous functions on $({\mathcal X},\mathop{\longrightarrow})$ which separates points in ${\mathcal X}$, then (\ref{eq:2}) defines a compatible metric that converts our space $({\mathcal X},\mathop{\longrightarrow})$ into a submetric space!
	
	Although the above scenario appears technically demanding, it was successfully implemented?using conditions ${\mathcal C}$ from Example~\ref{Ex:Stop}?in the construction of the so-called $S$ topology on the Skorokhod space \cite{Jak97b}. This topology, which is weaker than the more popular Skorokhod $J_{1}$ and $M_{1}$ topologies, has found significant applications, most recently in optimal martingale transport on the Skorokhod space (see, e.g., \cite{CKPS21, LiNe19}). Moreover, even the awareness of the nuances associated with the construction of submetric spaces from sequential spaces is slowly spreading (see, e.g., \cite{JAR26}).
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{Th:closure}
	In submetric spaces, the closure of a relatively compact subset $J$ coincides with the metric closure and consists of the limits of convergent sequences of elements of $J$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{Cor:relcomp}
	In a submetric space $({\mathcal X},\tau)$, if both $J$ and $\overline{J}$ are relatively $\tau$-compact, then $\overline{J}$ is $\tau$-compact.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
It follows from the above theorem that in a submetric space, for a c\`adl\`ag function  $x : [0,T] \to {\mathcal X}$, the closure of $V_x = \{x(t)\,|\,t \in [0,T]\}$ is $ K_x = \{ x(t)\, ; \, t\in [0,T]\} \cup \{ x(t-)\, ; \, t\in (0,T]\}$. Is it compact?
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{Ex:Jans}
	This is the example from \cite[Example 2.6]{Jan26}. Let $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ be the Smirnov space described in Example \ref{Ex:Smir}. Recall that $Z = \{ 1/n\,|\,n\in{\mathds{N}}\}$ is the non-typical closed set in ${\mathds{R}}^1$. Let $x : [0,1]\to {\mathcal X}$ be defined by
	\begin{equation}
		x(t) = \begin{cases} 
			0, &\text{if $x=0$};\\
			\frac{1}{2}(t+\frac{1}{n}), &\text{if $t \in [\frac{1}{n+1},\frac{1}{n})$}, n\in {\mathds{N}};\\
			1, &\text{if $x=1$}.
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
	Note that $V_x \cap Z = \emptyset $, while $K_x = [0,1]\supset Z$.  Since no subsequence of distinct elements of $Z$ is convergent, and $({\mathcal X}, \tau)$ is a submetric space, the set $K_x$ \emph{is not} $\tau$-compact  by Theorem \ref{thm_seqcomp}.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
The Smirnov space is, in several aspects, pathological among submetric spaces.  In what follows we shall restrict our attention to \emph{regular submetric spaces}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{Def:regsubmspace}
	We shall say that a topological space $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is \emph{a regular submetric space} if it is a submetric space and the closure $\overline{J}$ of each relatively $\tau$-compact space $J$ is $\tau$-compact.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
If $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is a regular submetric space, then for every c\'adl\`ag function $x :[0,T] \to {\mathcal X}$ the extended set of values $K_x = \{ x(t)\, ; \, t\in [0,T]\} \cup \{ x(t-)\, ; \, t\in (0,T]\}$ is $\tau$-compact.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
The existence of non-regular submetric spaces has a significant impact on the theory of limit theorems for stochastic processes. Let us return to the notion of the uniform tightness, discussed in Remark \ref{Rem:compare}. Recall that a family $\{X_{i}\}_{i\in{\mathds{I}}}$ of random elements with values in a submetric space $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is uniformly $\tau$-tight if  for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a $\tau$-compact set  $K_{\varepsilon}$ such that
	\[
	{\mathbb{P}}\big( X_i \in K_{\varepsilon} \big) > 1 - \varepsilon,\qquad i\in{\mathds{I}}.
	\]
	If $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is a regular submetric space, the above condition can be replaced with 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:nonreg}
		{\mathbb{P}}\big( X_i \in J_{\varepsilon} \big) > 1 - \varepsilon, \qquad i\in{\mathds{I}},
	\end{equation}
	where $J_{\varepsilon}$ is merely relatively $\tau$-compact. However, if $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ \emph{is not} a regular submetric space,  condition (\ref{eq:nonreg}) is strictly weaker than the uniform $\tau$-tightness.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{Th:lowersemi}
	Let $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ be a submetric space. Suppose we are given a family $\{h_i : {\mathcal X} \to [0,+\infty)\}_{i\in{\mathds{I}}}$ of {\em sequentially lower semicontinuous functionals} on $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ such that
	$J \subset {\mathcal X}$ is relatively $\tau$-compact if, and only if, 
	\[ \sup_{x\in J} h_i(x) < +\infty,\qquad i\in{\mathds{I}}.\]
	
	Then $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is a regular submetric space.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{Ex:Hilb2}
	Let us return to Example \ref{Ex:Hilb}. It is well-known  that a subset $J \subset {\mathds{H}}$ is relatively $\tau_w$-compact if, and only if, it is norm-bounded, i.e., 
	\[ \sup_{x\in J} \|x\| < +\infty.\]
	(See, e.g., the Eberlein-\v{S}mulyan theorem, \cite[Section V.6]{DunSch58}).
	Furthermore, the norm is sequentially lower semicontinuous.
	Indeed, if $x_n \ \mathop{\longrightarrow}_{\tau_w}\  x_0$, then for every $i\in {\mathds{N}}$ we have $\langle x_n,e_i\rangle \to \langle x_0,e_i\rangle$ and by the Fatou lemma
	\[ \liminf_{n\to\infty} \|x_n\|^2 = \liminf_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \langle x_n,e_i\rangle^2 \geq \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \langle x_0,e_i\rangle^2 = \|x_0\|^2.\]
	It then follows that $({\mathds{H}},\tau_w)$ is a regular submetric space.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{Ex:Stop}
	The $S$ topology on the Skorokhod space $\mathds{D} = \mathds{D}([0,T])$ of c\`adl\`ag functions $x : [0,T] \to {\mathds{R}}^1$ was constructed in  \cite{Jak97b}. We will define the set ${\mathcal C}$ of conditions (see Remark \ref{Rem:Intuition}) implying the relative compactness in the $S$ topology.
	
	Let us first introduce some relevant notation.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\|x\|_{\infty}$ is the uniform norm on $\mathds{D}$, i.e., $ \|x\|_{\infty} = \sup_{t\in [0,T]} |x(t)|$.
		\item 
		For $a < b$, $N^{a,b}(x)$ is \emph{the number of up-crossings of levels $a$ and $b$ by function $x\in \mathds{D}$}. In other words, $N^{a,b}(x)$ is the largest integer $k$ such that there are numbers  $0 \leq t_1 < t_2 <t_3 < \ldots < t_{2k-1} < t_{2k} \leq T$ satisfying $x(t_{2i - 1}) < a,\ x(t_{2i}) > b$, for each $i=1,2,\ldots, k$.
		\item For $\eta > 0$, $N_{\eta}(x)$ is \emph{the number of $\eta$-oscillations} of $x\in \mathds{D}$ on $[0,T]$. This means that $N_{\eta}(x)$ is the largest ineger $k$ such that there are numbers $0 \leq t_1 < t_2 \leq t_3 <  \ldots \leq  t_{2k-1} < t_{2k} \leq T$ satisfying $ \big|x(t_{2i}) - x(t_{2i - 1})\big| > \eta$, for each $i=1,2,\ldots, k$.
		\item $\|v\|(T)$ is \emph{the total variation of $v$ on $[0,T]$}:
		\[
		\|v\|(T)
		= \sup \big\{|v(0)| + \sum_{i=1}^{m} |v(t_i) - v(t_{i-1})|\big\}, \]
		where the supremum is taken over all 
		$0=t_0 < t_1 < \ldots < t_m = T,\ m\in{\mathds{N}}$.
		\item $\mathbb{V} = \big\{ x \in \mathds{D}\,;\, \|x\|(T) < +\infty\big\}$.
		\item If $v_{n,\varepsilon}, v_{0,\varepsilon} \in \mathbb{V}$, then  $v_{n,\varepsilon} \Rightarrow v_{0,\varepsilon}$ means that 
		\begin{equation}\label{evconvclear}
			\int_{[0,T]} f(t) \,dv_{n,\varepsilon}(t) \to \int_{[0,T]} f(t)\,dv_{0,\varepsilon}(t),
		\end{equation}
		for each continuous function $f : [0,T] \to {\mathds{R}}^1$. In particular, setting $f(t) \equiv 1$ we get
		\begin{equation}\label{vone}
			v_{n,\varepsilon}(T) \to v_{0,\varepsilon}(T).
		\end{equation}
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	The $S$ topology is a sequential topology defined via the $S$-convergence. 
	We shall write $x_n \ \mathop{\longrightarrow}_{S}\  x_0$
	if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ one can
	find elements $v_{n,\varepsilon}\in \mathds{V}$, $n=0,1,2,\ldots $ which are
	$\varepsilon$-uniformly close to $x_n$'s and weakly-$*$ convergent:
	\begin{eqnarray}
		\|x_n - v_{n,\varepsilon}\|_{\infty} \leq \varepsilon,&&\ n = 0, 1, 2,
		\ldots, \label{vclose}\\
		v_{n,\varepsilon} \Rightarrow v_{0,\varepsilon},&& \text{as $n\to\infty$}.\label{vconv}
	\end{eqnarray}
	Let us consider the following conditions describing properties of a subset $K\subset \mathds{D}$.
	\begin{align}
		\label{2e1}
		\sup_{x\in K}
		\|x\|_{\infty} &< +\infty. \\
		\label{2e2}
		\sup_{x\in K} N^{a,b}(x) &< +\infty,\quad \text{for all $a < b$}.\\
		\label{2e3}
		\sup_{x\in K} N_{\eta}(x) &< +\infty, \quad \text{for every $\eta > 0$}.
	\end{align}
	Then one can prove that either of the equivalent sets of conditions \ref{2e1} $+$ \ref{2e2} and  \ref{2e1} $+$ \ref{2e3} gives a criterion of relative $S$-compactness for $K$.
	
	Moreover, \cite[Corollary 2.10]{Jak97b} states that $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$, $N^{a,b}(\cdot)$ for $a < b$, and $N_{\eta}(\cdot)$ for $\eta > 0$ are sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to  $x_n \ \mathop{\longrightarrow}_{S}\  x_0$.
	
	We have thus found at least two candidates  
	for the family $\{h_i\}_{i\in{\mathds{I}}}$ in Theorem \ref{Th:lowersemi}.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
More general (but still applicable) sufficient conditions for $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ to be a regular submetric space can be found in \cite[Theorem 6.3]{Jak00}.
	
	In fact, the ideal situation would be if we could prove that a ``regular topological space'' that is also a ``submetric space'' yields a ``regular submetric space''.
	While we are unable to obtain such a result, we  provide two partial results in this direction.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
Let $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ be a submetric space and a regular topological space. Suppose that either of the following two conditions is satisfied: 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is sequential.
		\item $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is first-countable (i.e., at each point, there is a countable local basis).
	\end{enumerate}
	Then $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is a regular submetric space.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ be a Hausdorff space and let $x: [0,T] \to {\mathcal X}$ be a c\`adl\`ag function. Define 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:revers}
		y_x(t) := x(t-),\quad \text{ if $t\in (0,T]$};\qquad y_x(0) = x(0).
	\end{equation}
	We will say that $x$ is {\em reversibly } c\`adl\`ag, if $y$ is c\`agl\`ad, i.e., left continuous on $[0,T]$ and with limits form the right at $t\in [0,T)$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{Th:revers} If $x$ is  reversibly c\`adl\`ag, then $K_x$ is $\tau$-compact in ${\mathcal X}$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{Lem1}
		$B$ is at most finite.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{Lem1}, let  $B = \{ t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_m\}$.
	By (\ref{aje1}), for every $j=1,2,\ldots,m$ there exist: $\alpha_j,\beta_j \in A$ and 
	$\varepsilon_j > 0, \delta_j > 0$ such that
	\begin{eqnarray*}
		x(t_j) \in U_{\alpha_j},&& x(s) \in U_{\alpha_j}, s\in (t_j,t_j + \varepsilon_j),\\
		x(t_j-) \in U_{\beta_j} && x(s) \in U_{\beta_j}, s\in (t_j-\delta_j,t_j).
	\end{eqnarray*}
	
	Let us consider 
	\[ B_1 = [0,T] \setminus \Big( \bigcup_{j=1}^{m} (t_j-\delta_j,t_j+\varepsilon_j)\Big) \subset
	[0,T] \setminus B \subset S.\]
	$B_1$ is compact, hence we can find a finite set of ``good'' intervals $(a_l,b_l), \ l=1,2,\ldots, q$ and 
	$\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\ldots,\gamma_q \in A$ such that
	\[ x(s) \in U_{\gamma_l},\ s\in (a_l,b_l), l = 1,2, \ldots, q,\]
	and
	\[ B_1 \subset \bigcup_{l=1}^{q} (a_l,b_l).\]
	
	Hence the sum 
	\[ \bigcup_{j=1}^m U_{\alpha_j} \cup \bigcup_{j=1}^{m} U_{\beta_j} \cup \bigcup_{l=1}^{q} U_{\gamma_l}
	\]
	provides a finite covering of $\{ x(t)\,;\, t\in [0,T]\}$ {\em plus}, perhaps,  some $x(t-)$. Example \ref{Ex:Jans} shows that some $x(t-)$ may be not included in this subcover.
	Therefore we repeat the procedure for $y_x(t)$ and get  another finite covering 
	\[ \bigcup_{u=1}^{m'} U_{\alpha_u'} \cup \bigcup_{u=1}^{m'} U_{\beta_u'} \cup \bigcup_{v=1}^{q'} U_{\gamma_v'}
	\]
	of $\{ y(t)\,;\,t\in [0,T]\}$ plus some $y(t+) = x(t)$. Merging these two families we obtain a finite cover of $K_x$.
$\Box$
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
Janson's example shows that not all c\`adl\`ag functions are reversibly c\`adl\`ag.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
If $({\mathcal X},\tau)$ is a completely regular space and $x$ is a c\`adl\`ag function with values in ${\mathcal X}$, then
	$x$ is reversibly c\`adl\`ag. In particular, the set $K_x$ is $\tau$-compact.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
